source.title_on_document: Scanvas: Discovering and Developing Synergistic Opportunities in Generative Design Spaces

supplement.where: Section 7 Appendix at the end of this PDF
supplement.holds: Tutorial details, Creativity Support Index items for the Scanvas condition (Table 5), and AUT fluency correlations (Table 6); no extra statistics for the idea-quality contrasts

paper_design_summary: Study 1 compares an automated generation pipeline with no-expansion and no-synergy ablations, producing 90 ideas rated by two engineering experts (p. 10, Section 4.1). Study 2 is an in-person, counterbalanced within-person comparison in which the same 12 engineers used Scanvas and a baseline canvas with zero-shot GPT-5.5 prompts for 30 minutes per condition; randomized assignment is not stated (pp. 10-11, Sections 4.2-4.2.3). Two blind experts rated the submitted ideas, and semantic spread and idea counts were compared (pp. 12-16, Sections 4.2.4 and 5.1).

studies.label: Study 2: within-subject user study of the interactive system

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two systems (Scanvas vs. baseline) and which design task (Task 2 or 3) went with each system; counterbalanced across participants
assignment.quote: To reduce potential confounds from task content, fatigue and order effects, we counterbalanced task assignment, condition assignment, and presentation order across the 12 participants.

arms.name: Scanvas
arms.description: Full Scanvas canvas with idea enrichment and automatic synergy discovery (GPT-5.5)

arms.name: Baseline
arms.description: Similar canvas without automatic synergy discovery; Expand and +Mix used zero-shot GPT-5.5 prompts

participants.who: 7 full-time industry engineers and 5 engineering PhD students, all with professional industry experience (robotics, electrical engineering, related fields); recruited via Slack and email; mean 3.3 years in current role
participants.quote: We recruited 12 participants (7 men and 5 women) through professional networks via Slack and email.
participants.locator: p. 11, Section 4.2.2; p. 14, Fig. 5 legend (12 participants per condition)

ai_tool.name_model: Scanvas vs. baseline canvas, both on GPT-5.5
ai_tool.how_used: Participants added, expanded, and combined idea cards on a canvas; Scanvas also decomposed ideas and searched for synergistic combinations, while the baseline used zero-shot prompts to generate variants and combine ideas

task.description: Develop design concepts from three seed ideas for Task 2 (cooking support for an older adult with mild cognitive decline) or Task 3 (communicating artworks' visual style to visitors with visual impairments)
task.duration: 30-minute main task per condition; about 90-minute session

outcomes.name: Composite expert idea-quality rating (mean of Goal Fulfillment, New Benefits/Opportunities, Value vs. Cost, Interestingness; 7-point scale)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same two engineering experts used in the automated evaluation independently rated ideas on a 7-point scale, blind to condition and participant information (pp. 10 and 12, Sections 4.1 and 4.2.4). Figure 5 reports the experts' average ratings of ideas: 58 Scanvas ideas and 53 Baseline ideas from the same 12 participants (p. 14). The main comparisons are idea-level, using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests with Holm correction (p. 13, Section 5.1.2). The composite is the mean of Goal Fulfillment, New Benefits/Opportunities, Value vs. Cost, and Interestingness (p. 14, Figure 5).

contrasts.reported: Composite score: Scanvas M = 4.93, SD = 0.76; baseline M = 3.99, SD = 0.66, p < .001 (two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests with Holm correction); Scanvas 58 ideas, Baseline 53 ideas, 12 participants each

outcomes.name: Expert rating of overall interestingness (7-point scale)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same two engineering experts used in the automated evaluation independently rated ideas on a 7-point scale, blind to condition and participant information (pp. 10 and 12, Sections 4.1 and 4.2.4). Figure 5 reports the experts' average ratings of ideas: 58 Scanvas ideas and 53 Baseline ideas from the same 12 participants (p. 14). The main comparisons are idea-level, using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests with Holm correction (p. 13, Section 5.1.2). Interestingness means whether an idea is compelling and worth further exploration as a direction for continued design development; it is not defined as overall creativity (p. 10, Section 4.1).

contrasts.reported: overall interestingness (5.03 vs. 3.89, p < .001), Scanvas vs. baseline, two-sided Mann-Whitney U with Holm correction

outcomes.name: Semantic spread: mean pairwise cosine distance among ideas within each task and condition, averaged over the two tasks
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: The semantic spread of all submitted idea texts pooled within task and condition, averaged across the two user-study tasks. Higher mean pairwise cosine distance indicates more semantic diversity (p. 12, Section 4.2.4). The unit is a condition-level idea set; the 58 and 53 counts are ideas, not participants (p. 16, Table 4).

contrasts.reported: Scanvas: n ideas 58, semantic spread 0.564, 95% CI [0.513, 0.595]; Baseline: n ideas 53, semantic spread 0.534, 95% CI [0.477, 0.559]. Confidence intervals bootstrap participants. The Baseline row has no significance star: no significant Scanvas-Baseline difference is indicated after Holm correction across the four comparisons with Scanvas. The exact p-value, test statistic, and test procedure for that contrast are not supplied.

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine distance (higher means more diverse)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All submitted ideas pooled within each task and condition; mean distance over all idea pairs, then averaged across the two user-study tasks (p. 12, Section 4.2.4).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap confidence intervals resampling participants for the user-study conditions; comparisons against Scanvas receive Holm correction across four comparisons. No exact p-value, statistic, or test procedure is supplied for Scanvas versus Baseline (p. 16, Table 4).
diversity_detail.notes: A condition-level set measure across participants, not within-person flexibility. Reported values are raw cosine distances, not standardized effects. The 58 Scanvas and 53 Baseline ideas came from the same 12 participants (p. 14, Figure 5; p. 16, Table 4).

outcomes.name: Expert rating of Goal Fulfillment (7-point scale)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same two engineering experts used in the automated evaluation independently rated ideas on a 7-point scale, blind to condition and participant information (pp. 10 and 12, Sections 4.1 and 4.2.4). Figure 5 reports the experts' average ratings of ideas: 58 Scanvas ideas and 53 Baseline ideas from the same 12 participants (p. 14). The main comparisons are idea-level, using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests with Holm correction (p. 13, Section 5.1.2). How well the idea addresses the original design goal (p. 10, Section 4.1).

contrasts.reported: Goal Fulfillment: Scanvas M = 5.16 versus Baseline M = 4.50, p = .001; two-sided Mann-Whitney U test with Holm correction. Scanvas 58 ideas and Baseline 53 ideas, from the same 12 participants.

outcomes.name: Expert rating of New Benefits/Opportunities (7-point scale)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same two engineering experts used in the automated evaluation independently rated ideas on a 7-point scale, blind to condition and participant information (pp. 10 and 12, Sections 4.1 and 4.2.4). Figure 5 reports the experts' average ratings of ideas: 58 Scanvas ideas and 53 Baseline ideas from the same 12 participants (p. 14). The main comparisons are idea-level, using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests with Holm correction (p. 13, Section 5.1.2). Additional benefits or opportunities beyond the original goal; called New Opportunities in Section 4.1 and New Possibilities in Section 4.2.4. A participant-level robustness check separately compares each person's mean ratings; it does not supply participant-level precision for the main idea-level contrast (pp. 10, 12-13).

contrasts.reported: New Benefits/Opportunities: Scanvas M = 5.06 versus Baseline M = 4.27, p < .001; two-sided Mann-Whitney U test with Holm correction. Scanvas 58 ideas and Baseline 53 ideas, from the same 12 participants. The paper reports ratings of 6 or 7 for 34.5% of Scanvas ideas versus 3.8% of Baseline ideas. Participant-level check: 8 of 12 participants had higher mean ratings with Scanvas and four tied; Wilcoxon signed-rank p = .0078 among the eight non-tied participants.

outcomes.name: Number of ideas explored on the canvas per participant
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of ideas explored on the canvas during each system-assisted task; includes ideas explored rather than only the subset submitted for expert evaluation. These are participant-level counts from the same 12 people in both conditions (pp. 10-11, Sections 4.2-4.2.2; pp. 13-14, Section 5.1.2).

contrasts.reported: Scanvas M = 33.8 ideas, SD = 8.9; Baseline M = 26.3 ideas, SD = 7.8. The paper states no significant difference between conditions, without an exact p-value or test statistic. Same 12 participants in both conditions.

outcomes.name: Number of ideas submitted for evaluation per participant
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of ideas each participant recorded for later assessment, distinct from all ideas explored on the canvas. Participant-level paired comparison of the same 12 people (p. 11, Sections 4.2.1-4.2.2; p. 14, Section 5.1.2 and Figure 5).

contrasts.reported: Scanvas M = 4.83 ideas, SD = 1.27; Baseline M = 4.42 ideas, SD = 1.38; Wilcoxon signed-rank W = 8.5, p = .347. Same 12 participants in both conditions; 58 Scanvas and 53 Baseline ideas in total.

assignment.quote: All three conditions started from the same three seed ideas and produced 10 final ideas per task.

arms.description: Idea expansion followed by structured synergy generation and LLM selection of final ideas.

arms.name: No expansion
arms.description: Original seed ideas go directly to structured synergy generation without the expansion stage.

arms.name: No synergy
arms.description: Expansion retained; structured synergy generation replaced by direct LLM prompting for interesting idea combinations.

eligibility.reason: Study 2 analyzed the same 12 people in both conditions, below the 50-person criterion; the 58 Scanvas and 53 Baseline ideas are not additional participants (p. 11, Section 4.2.2; p. 14, Figure 5). Both arms used GPT-5.5, and task, condition, and presentation order were counterbalanced; the full document does not establish randomized assignment (pp. 10-11, Sections 4.2-4.2.3; Appendix 7, pp. 23-24). Independent expert ratings and embedding-based semantic spread are scored on outputs (p. 12, Section 4.2.4). Study 1 is model-only; its two experts are raters and its 90 observations are ideas, not people assigned to assistance (p. 10, Section 4.1). This paper remains screening-only: it supplies neither an eligible core study nor unassisted human-versus-AI output, observational, or synthesis context.

one_line_finding: In a within-subject study of 12 engineers, ideas developed with Scanvas received higher composite expert ratings than ideas from a zero-shot GPT-5.5 canvas baseline (M = 4.93 vs. 3.99 on a 7-point scale, p < .001, idea-level Mann-Whitney U; p. 13, Section 5.1.2).
notes: Study IDs are retained for audit continuity: S1 denotes the paper's Study 2 user study; the appended S2 denotes its Study 1 model-only evaluation. User-study expert ratings are analyzed at idea level, while Figure 4 plots individual ratings for the model-only evaluation. Per-arm idea counts are retained in reported results; no unprinted total observation counts or effect sizes are computed. The participant-level New Benefits check is retained within that outcome. Participant self-reports of creativity support, feature usefulness, and perceived idea quality are not treated as independently scored output outcomes (pp. 11-12, Section 4.2.4; Figures 7-9; p. 24, Table 5). The pre-study AUT and its correlations describe baseline ability, not an AI-removed outcome (pp. 16 and 24, Section 5.1.4 and Table 6). Cross-study comparisons of user-assisted ideas with automated ideas (pp. 15-16, Section 5.1.3) are not additional human-assistance experiments.
